subject: Fitting an Poisson regression that is not identified

messages.author: 5a363da2ae84b3c2
messages.subject: Fitting an Poisson regression that is not identified
parts:
Hello fellow stan users,

I’m writing to solicit suggestions for improving the speed of sampling from my model.

I am interested in fitting the following model

y ~ Poisson(theta_j*q_j)

where theta_j is a positive number and q_j is a probability, indexed by j groups of observations. The goal of this project to (eventually) estimate both theta_j and q_j as linear functions of predictors under transformation, but at the moment I am struggling with the simpler task of efficiently estimating the constant term for each. (In my notation, theta=exp(X*beta) and logit(q)=Z*gamma, where X and Z are matrices of covariates and beta and gamma are vectors of coefficients, but this is only relevant to the future task of estimating coefficient terms.)

Clearly, one source of difficulty for this model is that it is not identified because there are infinitely many pairs theta, q which have the same product. Taking the tips from “Problematic Posteriors” section of the stan modeling reference, I’ve attempted to identify this model via prior specification. I believe that the model is sufficiently identified that it must be proper (though perhaps I have missed a subtlety which is preventing efficient runtime).

Simulated data for j=4 achieved R_hat <1.1 in 1500 iterations, taking between 570 and 670 seconds total per chain; however, n_eff is in the dozens for some parameter estimates. However, posterior medians are reasonably near the true values of the parameters for a synthetic data created with known, fixed theta and q, so I believe that the model is identified.

In simulated data, a plot of theta, q pairs clearly fall in a “sharply bent cigar” pattern. I believe that this might be the source of the problem: while stan is able to identify the “ridge” for which the product theta*q is plausible for a given y, it is difficult to sample from within that shape, likely since its contours are so stark. If the sampler steps in the wrong direction, it falls into the abyss. This implies a re-parameterization might be in order.

I’ve advanced my line of thinking this far: since we know mean(y) is the MLE for the Poisson distribution, deriving this quantity for each sector might go quite far in eliminating some wasteful rejections or wanderings, since “discovering” mean(y) reveals the best “ridge” along which sampling should be conducted. This implies that we want to conduct sampling along the line ln(mean(y))=ln(theta)+ln(q) that falls in the vicinity of the prior. But this is as far as I’ve gotten. Additionally, I’m concerned that this “trick” might not generalize well in the case when I’m trying to fit more than just an intercept: figuring out how to sample in a space near ln(mean(y))=X*beta-log(1+exp(-Z*gamma)) seems difficult, but perhaps I simply lack imagination.

V/r,

David Elkind

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting an Poisson regression that is not identified
parts:
A problem that can arise in very weakly identified models, by
which I mean ones where the posterior mean or median is
technically identified, but the posterior is relatively flat
around the mean. There's a discussion in the manual in the
problematic posteriors chapter.

The usual solution is to tighten priors. This can almost always
be done with very little affect on the solutions --- that is,
going from a very vague prior to one that's weakly informative.
For example normal(0,5) for a logistic regression coefficient compared
to normal(0,100) will make a big difference in computation without
affecting the posterior distribution much at all (assuming the predictor's
standardized and the data's not separable or close to it), especially in
cases where there's not much data.

Weak hyperpriors can cause the same kind of problem, with broad
swaths of the posterior having similar density, requiring a lot
of work to explore for the sampler.

More specifics below.

> Hello fellow stan users,

The goal of this project to (eventually) estimate both theta_j and q_j as linear functions of predictors under transformation, but at the moment I am struggling with the simpler task of efficiently estimating the constant term for each. (In my notation, theta=exp(X*beta) and logit(q)=Z*gamma, where X and Z are matrices of covariates and beta and gamma are vectors of coefficients, but this is only relevant to the future task of estimating coefficient terms.)

Depending on values, it might be more stable to work on the log scale.

y ~ poisson_log(X*beta + log_inv_logit(Z * gamma));

where we have

poisson_log(y|alpha) = poisson(y|exp(alpha))

>
> Clearly, one source of difficulty for this model is that it is not identified because there are infinitely many pairs theta, q which have the same product. Taking the tips from “Problematic Posteriors” section of the stan modeling reference, I’ve attempted to identify this model via prior specification. >
> Simulated data for j=4 achieved R_hat <1.1 in 1500 iterations, taking between 570 and 670 seconds total per chain; however, n_eff is in the dozens for some parameter estimates. However, posterior medians are reasonably near the true values of the parameters for a synthetic data created with known, fixed theta and q, so I believe that the model is identified.

You may find with more data that you get a better behaved
posterior.

>
> In simulated data, a plot of theta, q pairs clearly fall in a “sharply bent cigar” pattern. I believe that this might be the source of the problem: while stan is able to identify the “ridge” for which the product theta*q is plausible for a given y, it is difficult to sample from within that shape, likely since its contours are so stark. If the sampler steps in the wrong direction, it falls into the abyss. This implies a re-parameterization might be in order.

Reparameterization can often help. The problem with
banana-like densities is that their curvature varies
over their support, making it impossible to properly
adapt Euclidean HMC as used in Stan. The result is that
you have to use smaller step sizes to get accurate
results (in practice, set the acceptance target higher to
make sure you're getting stable results).
> I’ve advanced my line of thinking this far:
Plotting the posterior to see what's going on is most of the battle!

> since we know mean(y) is the MLE for the Poisson distribution, deriving this quantity for each sector might go quite far in eliminating some wasteful rejections or wanderings, since “discovering” mean(y) reveals the best “ridge” along which sampling should be conducted. This implies that we want to conduct sampling along the line ln(mean(y))=ln(theta)+ln(q) that falls in the vicinity of the prior. But this is as far as I’ve gotten. Additionally, I’m concerned that this “trick” might not generalize well in the case when I’m trying to fit more than just an intercept: figuring out how to sample in a space near ln(mean(y))=X*beta-log(1+exp(-Z*gamma)) seems difficult, but perhaps I simply lack imagination.

In my experience, adding an intercept can often help immensely
in these models if you don't already have a column of 1 values
in X to act as an intercept.

Keep in mind that everything samples on the unconstrained parameters in Stan,
and that's where you want to look for nice covexity and peakiness
properties.

Others are better at this kind of thing than me.
If you create another post that just has a tight model definition
and asks about reparameterizations, Andrew or Michael or Ben can
probably help out.

- Bob

This implies that we want to conduct sampling along the line ln(mean(y))=ln(theta)+ln(q) that falls in the vicinity of the prior. But this is as far as I’ve gotten. Additionally, I’m concerned that this “trick” might not generalize well in the case when I’m trying to fit more than just an intercept: figuring out how to sample in a space near ln(mean(y))=X*beta-log(1+exp(-Z*gamma)) seems difficult, but perhaps I simply lack imagination.

I'm also pasting the model inline here for others who may have missed the
attachment in case anyone has ideas for reparameterization:

data{
int<lower=1> num_sectors;
int<lower=1> N;
int<lower=1> sector_id[N];
int<lower=0> y[N];
}
parameters{
real beta0_mu;
real<lower=0, upper=10> beta0_tau;
vector[num_sectors] beta0_eta;

real gamma0_mu;
real<lower=0, upper=10> gamma0_tau;
vector[num_sectors] gamma0_eta;
}
transformed parameters{
vector[N] log_inv_logit_q_hat;
vector[N] log_theta_hat;

vector[num_sectors] beta0;
vector[num_sectors] gamma0;
vector[N] ln_y_hat;

beta0 <- beta0_mu+beta0_tau*beta0_eta;

gamma0 <- gamma0_mu+gamma0_tau*gamma0_eta;

for(n in 1:N){
log_inv_logit_q_hat[n] <- log_inv_logit(gamma0[sector_id[n]]);
log_theta_hat[n] <- beta0[sector_id[n]];
}
ln_y_hat <- log_inv_logit_q_hat+log_theta_hat;
}
model{
beta0_eta ~ normal(0,1);
gamma0_mu ~ student_t(3,0,5);
gamma0_eta ~ normal(0,1);
y ~ poisson_log(ln_y_hat);
}

I didn't notice the model the first time and now I
see you are working on the log scale. And that you have
relatively tight priors (assuming the scales are around 1).
Nice!

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting an Poisson regression that is not identified
parts: I think that there is actually two levels of "non identification" in the current model. The first one is, as you say, that there is infinitely many pairs of theta and q. But the second one is due that q and theta are modelled as a linear function of other parameters (no data involved), ie:

beta0  <- beta0_mu+beta0_tau*beta0_eta;
    gamma0 <- gamma0_mu+gamma0_tau*gamma0_eta;

So actually now there is many different beta0_mu, beta0_tau and beta0_eta triples giving the same values for beta0 as well (and similarly for gamma0). In the final model, if I understood correctly, beta0_eta and gamma0_eta would be data, right? That would be better, as it eliminates at least this problem.

messages.author: 5a363da2ae84b3c2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting an Poisson regression that is not identified
parts:
The goal of enumerating beta0 and gamma0 in this way is to allow for a hierarchical structure to the model, so that beta0[j] refers to the jth grouping (sector) of observations. *_mu is the mean of these group-level effects, while *_eta and *_tau allow the direction and magnitude of the effect to vary for each sector, while still restricting it to be somewhere near *_mu.

This explanation is not mutually exclusive with your proposal being correct, though. Perhaps it is simply expensive to simultaneously identify both theta and q AND the hierarchical structure at the same time. I had hoped that the hierarchical structure would help enforce some regularity across sectors, thereby making it easier to estimate theta and q, but the cost is, of course, introducing additional free parameters, so perhaps it's a wash.

Yes, of course. I was misreading the model a bit (somehow thought that there were many mu/tau). So basically you just have the usual hierarchical priors (but reparametrized version):
  beta0[k] ~ normal(beta0_mu,beta0_tau)
  gamma0[k] ~ normal(gamma0_mu,gamma0_tau)
